solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Can it split? Confess

parts.note: 'can it!' is slang for 'be quiet!', which is SH
to rive is an old word for to split or tear apart

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a tin will burst, followed by a one-word plea to own up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a tin; 'can it' is the command to shut up. To shrive is strictly to hear confession and absolve, but it can also mean to confess.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrive is an old church word for making or hearing a confession of sins.

clue.text: Poet, the scoundrel, pinching almost all of another

indicators.note: pinching means holding tight, so the scoundrel's letters hold the other poet

parts.note: swine is an insult for a scoundrel

indicators.note: almost all of means the other poet's name loses its final letter

parts.note: another poet: Robert Burns

explanation.surface: One poet calls another a scoundrel for stealing nearly all his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinching' looks like stealing but means holding inside; 'another' means another poet, the Scot Robert Burns, trimmed by 'almost all of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Charles Swinburne was a Victorian English poet.

clue.text: Pushed back, gave another performance?

definitions.meaning: the question mark flags the split

explanation.surface: An actor resisted, then went on stage again.
explanation.definitionFit: To react is to respond in opposition, while re-act means to perform once more.

clue.text: See a street in depression

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for vide, Latin for see
an alley is a narrow street

explanation.surface: Someone notices a street lying in a hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' looks like low mood; it is a dip in the land.
explanation.definitionFit: A valley is a low area of land between hills, a depression in the ground.

clue.text: Piled in heap, dogs off lead showed visible distress

indicators.note: a dog off its lead has lost what goes in front, so the word for the dogs drops its leading letter

parts.note: young dogs are pups
to weep is to show distress visibly; wept is the past tense

explanation.surface: Dogs let loose after a heap of something was piled up, and someone wept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off lead' looks like dogs unleashed in a park; it means PUPS loses its first letter, giving UPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Upswept describes hair or similar swept upwards and gathered high, as if piled on top.

clue.text: To set free, amputate limb?

definitions.meaning: a peg is a wooden leg, so ... playfully means remove a limb

explanation.surface: A grim question about freeing someone by cutting off a leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpeg means unfasten by removing pegs; a peg leg makes the joke reading.

clue.text: Sort of bob, remarkably sleek fashion

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something unusual done to the word, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: ton is an old word for fashion or style

explanation.surface: A haircut, a sort of bob, styled remarkably sleek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bob' looks like a haircut; it is a bobsleigh, and skeleton is a head-first sled event.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeleton is a winter sled sport, related to bobsleigh, ridden head-first.

clue.text: What spoils the view at heart of storm is very concerning

parts.note: the eye is the calm centre of a storm
a sore point is one that is very troubling

explanation.surface: What wrecks a view at the centre of a storm is deeply worrying.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is an ugly thing that spoils a scene.

clue.text: Now daughter comes in for a hot drink

indicators.note: comes in for means takes the place of the other letter

parts.note: today means now, at the present time

explanation.surface: A daughter arriving now for a warming drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes in for' swaps the A of TODAY for D.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot drink of spirits, sugar and water.

clue.text: Roughly haul about somewhat, as usual

indicators.note: about means the rearranged word goes round the other piece
roughly means not exactly, so the word's letters are shaken into another order

parts.note: 'a bit' means somewhat, slightly

explanation.surface: Hauling something roughly about, which is what usually happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' looks like 'approximately' but signals the anagram; 'about' means around, putting the shuffled word round the phrase for somewhat.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual describes what is customary or done by habit, regularly.

clue.text: Totalled up at last, with no case

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: finally means at last

explanation.surface: A sum finally added up, with a lawsuit dropped along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no case' strips the first and last letters from FINALLY, leaving the inner letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase in all gives the overall total, as in 'twenty pounds in all'.

clue.text: Understand program, run with what purpose?

parts.note: an app is a computer program
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
'eh?' is a way of saying 'what?'
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: A puzzled user tries to grasp a software routine and asks what running it is for.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing question mark marks 'what' as the exclamation 'eh?', not an ordinary question word.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprehend can mean to grasp mentally, a formal synonym of understand.

clue.text: Feasting greedily in club, liable to waste days

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport

indicators.note: to waste here means to lose, so the word for liable lets a letter slip away

parts.note: tending (to) means liable or inclined to

explanation.surface: Someone gorging at their club, apt to fritter away whole days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liable to' reads as one phrase but 'to waste' is the deletion signal; 'in' simply links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To batten on something is to gorge or thrive greedily at its expense.

clue.text: Resin you once put back to inhibit disease

indicators.note: inhibit is read as holding in, so the reversed pronoun goes around the illness
put back means the old word for you is turned round

parts.note: ye is an archaic word for you
pox is a disease

explanation.surface: An old remedy: a resin you once applied to hold an illness at bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' reverses the old pronoun to EY, and 'to inhibit' reads as restraining: those two letters hold the disease between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Epoxy is a synthetic resin used in strong adhesives and coatings.

clue.text: Try again to get out of fire door

indicators.note: letters are taken out of the words that follow, a run of letters lifted from inside them

explanation.surface: Someone stuck behind a fire door has another go at escaping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get out of' signals letters lifted from inside 'fire door'.
explanation.definitionFit: To redo something is to do it again, another attempt at it.

clue.text: One curate I trained who has lots to deal with

definitions.text: who has lots to deal with

indicators.note: trained means schooled or drilled into shape, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A parish priest boasts of training a curate who now has plenty on his plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lots' looks like a heavy workload; it means the numbered items at a sale.
explanation.definitionFit: An auctioneer sells goods in numbered lots, so has lots to deal with.

clue.text: English avoiding wooden ware getting expensive French plate

indicators.note: avoiding means the letter for English is kept out of the word

parts.note: treen is household ware made of wood
cher is the French word for expensive

explanation.surface: Fine French tableware chosen over English wooden pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding' takes an E out of TREEN, leaving TREN.
explanation.definitionFit: A trencher is an old wooden plate or board for serving food.

clue.text: Obscure playground rumour finally true

parts.note: rec is short for recreation ground, a playground
on dit (French, 'they say') is a piece of gossip

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A schoolyard rumour that turns out true after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Recondite means abstruse, little known, hard to understand.

clue.text: East European and American statesman are going out

definitions.note: read as American state's man: a man from Georgia in America, and someone from Georgia in eastern Europe

indicators.note: out suggests the words are put out of shape, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An Eastern European and a US politician head off for an evening together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'statesman' looks like a politician; split it as state's man, a man from the US state of Georgia. 'out' rearranges ARE GOING.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgia is both a Caucasian country and a US state, and a native of either is a Georgian.

clue.text: Spring flowers I left out in winds

indicators.note: out means these letters are left out of the flowers' name

parts.note: Easter lilies are flowers of spring

explanation.surface: Spring flowers blown about in the wind, with one left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes I and L from EASTER LILIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Easterlies are winds blowing from the east.

clue.text: Show exasperation after missing a fine practice shot

parts.note: to sigh is to show exasperation

indicators.note: missing means these letters are absent from the word

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: A shooter sighs in frustration after missing with a trial shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' looks like a placement signal but is itself the word that loses letters, as 'missing' says.
explanation.definitionFit: A sighter is a trial shot fired to check the aim before scoring begins.

clue.text: Style of greeting in cricket club

indicators.note: in means the greeting goes inside the club's initials

parts.note: hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A cricket club with a particular way of welcoming people.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic means stylish elegance, so it is a word for style.

clue.text: Emergency provision in hotel out of order

indicators.note: out of order means not in the proper sequence, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hotel's emergency equipment is not working.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotline is a direct phone line kept ready for emergencies.

clue.text: Green plant round field regularly makes fodder

indicators.note: round means the herb's letters go around the other letters

parts.note: sage is a green herb

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A green plant growing round a field ends up as animal feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes I and L from 'field'.
explanation.definitionFit: Silage is fermented green crop stored as winter feed for livestock.

clue.text: Better to make this payment with rupees

parts.note: a wage is a payment for work

explanation.surface: A payment made in rupees, presented as an improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like 'preferable'; it is one who bets, and what a bettor makes is a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: A bettor makes a wager, a stake on an outcome, so the definition describes it.

clue.text: Strange hold-up in river delta

parts.note: a weir is a low dam that holds back a river
delta is D in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A blockage in the river at its delta.
explanation.definitionFit: Weird means odd or uncanny, a synonym of strange.

clue.text: Church official has wrapped silks, brown, for chapter to wear

indicators.note: the garments are said to wear the letter, so it goes inside them

parts.note: saris are garments of silk wrapped round the body
tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: A church official laying out brown silks for the cathedral chapter to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for chapter to wear' puts C inside SARIS, giving SACRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacristan is the church officer in charge of the sacristy and its vestments.

clue.text: Nick's small cloth

parts.note: a wipe is a cleaning cloth

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick owns a small cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name; it is the verb meaning steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick and swipe are both informal words meaning steal.

clue.text: Some northerners grasp tons I have not taught

indicators.note: grasp means the people's name holds the letter inside it

parts.note: the Inuit are peoples of the Arctic north
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: Some northerners grasping tons of knowledge that nobody taught them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grasp' puts T inside INUIT, making INTUIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Intuitive knowledge is known by instinct rather than learnt from instruction.

clue.text: Excuse one replacing a graduate in panto role

indicators.note: replacing means the numeral takes the place of the graduate in the character's name

parts.note: Ali Baba is a character in Christmas pantomime
A plus BA, a Bachelor of Arts graduate
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An excuse offered when one actor takes over a graduate's part in the panto.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is a British family Christmas stage show based on fairy tales. 'replacing' swaps the closing ABA of ALI BABA for I.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, used as an excuse.

clue.text: Disorder puts part of US hospital in no end of peril

indicators.note: in means the hospital department goes inside the other word
no end of means the word for peril loses its last letter

parts.note: danger means peril
ER is the emergency room of an American hospital

explanation.surface: Chaos in an American hospital department leaves endless danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts' is only a link; 'no end of' shortens the word for peril to DANGE before the department goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To derange is to throw into disorder or confusion, so the two verbs match.

clue.text: Show great respect for son escaping misfortune

indicators.note: escaping means the letter for son gets away from the word

parts.note: a reverse is a setback or misfortune

explanation.surface: A son who avoided bad luck is held in high regard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'escaping' takes the S out of REVERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere is to honour or venerate deeply.
